title: Ten skills worth writing.
subtitle: The ten I wrote for the people I teach, what each does, and a request to try:
text: I wrote ten Claude skills for the people I teach. Each one does one job, the way I'd want it done. Here's what they do, so you can write your own versions. What's inside: Two for learning Two for research Two for your career Two for everyday work One for data One that writes the others Learn and remember learn-anything A patient tutor for any topic. It asks what you already know and makes a short plan. Then it explains one idea at a time, with an analogy and a small example, and checks you understood before moving on. Teach me how neural networks learn. I know basic algebra. quiz-me Turns your notes, a document or a topic into practice questions, asked one at a time. It explains every answer, keeps track of what you miss and comes back to it. Quiz me on these lecture notes. Ten questions, mixed. Research and explain research-brief Answers a question with a one-page, sourced brief. It separates what's known from what's only claimed, gives each finding a confidence level and never invents a source. news-explainer Turns AI and tech news into a plain explainer: what happened, why it matters, who it affects and what's still unknown. Every claim is attributed. No hype. Explain this announcement for my newsletter readers. Grow your career linkedin-post Writes LinkedIn posts in your own voice, from an idea, a lesson or a piece of work. You get an opening worth reading, one clear point, and no invented stories or engagement bait. Turn this project I finished into a post. Here are two of my old posts. job-application Tailors your CV and cover letter to one job ad. It matches your real experience to what the employer asks for, and tells you honestly where the gaps are. Here's my CV and the job ad. Tailor both. Get work done meeting-to-actions Turns meeting notes or a transcript into decisions, actions with owners and deadlines, open questions and a follow-up email. It never invents an owner or a date. Here's the transcript of today's team call. presentation-planner Plans a talk before you open slide software: the story, one message per slide, titles that state the point, visuals and speaker notes. Plan a ten-minute talk on our quarterly results for the board. Work with data check-the-numbers Answers questions about spreadsheets, CSV files and SQL results, and proves the answer first. A script profiles each file for missing values, numbers stored as text, repeated rows and gaps in the dates. Every join is checked for multiplied rows. Which products drove last quarter's revenue? Here's the export. Make your own skill-maker Interviews you about a task you repeat, writes the SKILL.md, checks it against the rules and packages the folder as a zip, ready to upload. Help me turn the way I write our weekly report into a skill. Start with one Don't write ten. Pick the job you explain to Claude most often, and make that your first skill. issue:make-your-first-skill Mojeed

title: Make your first skill.
subtitle: Turn the instructions you paste most into a Claude skill, in five steps:
text: You've explained the same thing to Claude three times. That's your sign. It's time to make it a skill. A skill is a folder with one file in it. You write it once. Claude uses it every time a request needs it. Here's the whole process: Pick the task Write the SKILL.md Write the instructions Zip the folder Upload it and test it New to skills? Start with the guide Step 1: Pick the task Pick the job you explain most. The weekly report. The meeting summary. The client email in your team's format. One skill, one job. If you need two jobs, make two skills. I'll use a weekly report as the example below. Step 2: Write the SKILL.md Make a folder named after the skill: weekly-report. Inside it, make a file called SKILL.md. It starts with the name and the description, between two lines of dashes: --- name: weekly-report description: Turns the week's notes and numbers into our team's weekly report format. Use when someone asks for the weekly report or pastes weekly updates. --- The rules that matter: Part Rule Name Lowercase letters, numbers and hyphens. 64 characters at most. The same as the folder's name. Can't contain "claude" or "anthropic". Description What it does and when to use it, in the third person. 200 characters at most in the Claude apps. No tags in angle brackets. Claude decides when to use your skill from the description alone. Spend your time there. Step 3: Write the instructions Below the dashes, write how you want the job done. Keep it under 500 lines. Include: numbered steps the mistakes to avoid one short example a checklist, if the job is long Need a template or reference notes? Put them in the folder, link each one from SKILL.md, and say when to read it. Don't want to write it alone? Ask Claude to draft it with you: Help me turn the way I write our weekly report into a skill. Ask me questions first, then write the SKILL.md. Get the next guide by email Step 4: Zip the folder This is where most uploads fail. Zip the folder, not the files inside it. weekly-report/ ├── SKILL.md required: name, description and instructions ├── reference.md optional: detail Claude reads only when it needs it ├── templates/ optional: files to fill in └── scripts/ optional: code for steps that must be exact The zip must contain weekly-report/SKILL.md. If the files sit at the top of the zip without their folder, the upload won't work. Step 5: Upload it and test it Upload it: Customize → Skills → + → Create skill → Upload a skill. Check its switch is on. Then test it with five requests: Write three requests that should use the skill. Write two that shouldn't. Try all five. Did Claude miss one? Fix the description first. It's what Claude uses to choose. Three requests that should use it Two that shouldn't All five behave as expected What to do today Open the last chat where you pasted your usual instructions. Copy them into a SKILL.md. Add a name and a description. That's your first skill. guide:claude-skills-from-zero Send this to one colleague who still pastes the same prompt every morning. Mojeed

title: Claude skills, from zero.
subtitle: For anyone who pastes the same instructions into Claude every day: install your first skill safely and use it today.
text: You paste the same long instructions into Claude. You explain the same format again. You correct the same mistakes. A skill ends that. You teach Claude a job once, and it does it your way from then on. By the end of this guide you'll have: one skill installed and switched on a clear idea of when Claude uses it a short safety check you can run on any skill You need: a Claude account and ten minutes. 1. Know what a skill is A skill is a small folder of instructions. Sometimes it also holds scripts and templates. Every skill has one required file: SKILL.md. Its first lines hold two things: a name, which is also the command you can type, such as /learn-anything a description of what the skill does and when to use it Below that come the instructions: steps, rules, examples and checklists. Claude decides when to use a skill from its description alone. A clear description is the difference between a skill that works and one that sits there. 2. See how skills differ You already have other ways to shape Claude. Here's where a skill fits: Feature What it gives Claude When it applies Custom instructions Your general preferences Every conversation Projects Background documents and knowledge Chats inside that project Connectors (MCP) Access to other apps and data When Claude needs that app Skills A way of doing one job Only when a request needs it, in any chat They work well together. A connector lets Claude reach your project tracker. A skill teaches it how your team writes tickets. 3. Check where skills work Skills work in more places than most people think: Claude on the web and in the desktop app, on every plan from Free to Enterprise, once code execution is on. Claude Code, from folders on your computer. Claude for Excel, PowerPoint, Word and Outlook. Cowork, which uses the skills switched on for your account. The Claude API, in beta, where skills run in a sandbox with no internet access. Skills also follow an open standard, the Agent Skills specification. A skill you write isn't locked to one product. 4. Turn skills on Open Settings → Capabilities. Turn on Create and edit files. In the older Settings layout, it's called Code execution and file creation. On Team plans, skills are on by default. On Enterprise plans, an owner turns them on first, in Organization settings → Plugins & skills, on the Policy tab. 5. Install a skill There are two ways to get one. Ready-made: open Customize → Skills, click +, then Browse skills. You'll find skills from partners such as Notion, Figma and Atlassian, built to work with their connectors. From a zip (one you made, or one from a source you trust): Get the skill's zip file. Don't unzip it. Open Customize → Skills, click +, then Create skill → Upload a skill. Choose the zip. Check that the skill's switch is on. That's it. Ask for something the skill covers. Make your own skill 6. Use it You rarely need to do anything special. Claude reads the descriptions of your skills and uses one by itself when your request matches. To be sure, name it: Use my weekly-report skill on these notes. In Claude Code and in the Microsoft 365 add-ins, you can also type / and pick a skill from the list. Claude didn't use the skill you expected? Check that its switch is on, name it in your request, or make its description clearer about when it applies. 7. Add skills to Claude Code Claude Code reads skills from folders on your computer. For every project: unzip the skill into ~/.claude/skills/, so you end up with ~/.claude/skills/learn-anything/SKILL.md. For one project (and everyone who works on it): unzip it into the project's .claude/skills/ folder and commit it. Run a skill by typing a slash and its name, or just ask. /skills lists what's installed. Skills you switch on in your Claude account also sync to Claude Code when you sign in with the same account. 8. Stay safe A skill can contain code that runs when Claude uses it. So treat an unknown skill like an unknown app. Never put passwords, API keys or personal data in a skill. The two main risks: Prompt injection: hidden instructions that steer Claude into something you didn't ask for. Data leaks: a script that sends your information somewhere. The fix is the same for both: check before you trust. On Enterprise plans, owners can also turn on skill scanning, which checks uploaded skills for malicious content. Before you finish Create and edit files is on One skill is installed and its switch is on I read every file of that skill before switching it on I asked for something it covers, and Claude used it Questions Do many skills slow Claude down? No. Skills load in layers. Claude always sees just the name and description of each skill you've switched on, a line or two each. It reads the instructions only when a request matches, and extra files only if needed. When is a skill worth making? Once you've explained the same thing to Claude three times. Where can I learn from good examples? Anthropic's examples on GitHub, at github.com/anthropics/skills, are good to learn from and adapt. issue:make-your-first-skill
